request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Switchboard operator, male, 1st year

Interviewer: You came here from another part of the country. How are you getting on with your colleagues?

Interviewee: Really well. Everyone loves a joke. I’m from Guangdong and I’ve got a bit of an accent when I speak Mandarin, so my team leader gave me the nickname Little Canton, and now the whole front office calls me that. It sounds really friendly to me. Sometimes when guests from Hong Kong or Macau phone in, my colleagues shout, Little Canton, it’s for you, and I take the call in Cantonese. The guests are really pleased when they hear it, and one of them even wrote me a praise card specially. Later my team leader had me teach everyone a phrase of Cantonese at the morning briefing each week. Last week it was m goi, Cantonese for thank you. Everyone’s pronunciation was really strange, I couldn’t stop laughing, and they laughed too. One colleague wrote m goi on the back of their hand and practised it all day. At the last department dinner everyone was chatting in the local dialect. My team leader saw I couldn’t understand, so he got everyone to switch to Mandarin, and he even ordered a Cantonese dish specially, saying it was so Little Canton could have a taste of home. They go hiking together at weekends, and they added me to the group chat the very first time. That day everyone looked at their phones and laughed together at the photos of me hiking. I’d run out of steam halfway up, and two colleagues walked with me to the top, one in front and one behind. None of these jokes are mean-spirited, and I quite like them myself. Now I’m learning the local dialect from my colleagues too. It’s been almost three months, and I can understand more than half of it. Sometimes I even joke around with my team leader in the local dialect on purpose, and he says I’ve picked up bad habits. There’s a front-desk vacancy next month. My team leader encouraged me to apply. He said being able to speak two dialects is an advantage. I’ve already handed in my application.
